title: Kinetic temperatures and inertial effects in a nonequilibrium bead-spring model
authors: Jetin E Thomas, Ramandeep S. Johal
abstract: We investigate a nonequilibrium steady-state model consisting of two coupled beads with arbitrary masses in contact with two thermal baths at different temperatures. Using a covariance-matrix approach together with numerical simulations of the underdamped Langevin dynamics, we characterize steady-state probability distributions, heat transport, and entropy production. We show that irreversibility measures such as entropy production and heat current are invariant under an exchange of the bead masses, whereas energy-storage observables depend explicitly on the mass arrangement in a symmetrical set up. This reveals a fundamental distinction: energy observables exhibit path dependence in singular mass limits, while transport and irreversibility remain well defined. We show that kinetic temperatures provide the natural variables governing the thermodynamics of the system: their difference controls transport and entropy production, while their sum determines the mean energy via a model specific generalized equipartition relation. In the infinite-mass limit, only constitutive relations expressed in terms of kinetic temperatures remain meaningful. Thus, energy, transport, and irreversibility are unified through kinetic temperatures as the organizing variables. We also derive an effective temperature that defines an equilibrium-like canonical distribution. Finally, we analyze the notion of ergodicity and show that the time-averaged observables converge significantly faster than the ensemble averages.
summary: This work analyzes a two-bead model coupled to two baths at different temperatures to study nonequilibrium steady states. It establishes that kinetic temperatures are the fundamental variables governing the system's thermodynamics, unifying energy, heat transport, and entropy production. The findings highlight a crucial distinction between path-dependent energy observables and robust, temperature-governed transport measures.
main_problem: The paper investigates the characterization of nonequilibrium steady states (NESS) in coupled systems subjected to thermal baths at different temperatures, focusing on the role of inertia.
main_result: Kinetic temperatures are shown to be the fundamental organizing variables that unify energy, heat transport, and entropy production in the system.
method: The analysis employs a covariance-matrix approach combined with numerical simulations of underdamped Langevin dynamics to solve for steady-state properties.
model_or_system: The model is a bead-spring system consisting of two beads with arbitrary masses, coupled by a spring, and interacting independently with two thermal baths at distinct temperatures ($T_1$ and $T_2$).
key_observables: Steady-state probability distributions, heat transport ($\dot{Q}$), entropy production ($\Delta S_{tot}/	au$), and kinetic temperatures ($T_{kin}$).
important_parameters: Bead masses ($m_1, m_2$), spring constant ($\kappa$), and bath temperatures ($T_1, T_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed within a linear Langevin framework, and the results are shown to be robust for transport/irreversibility measures even when energy observables show path dependence in singular mass limits.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the two beads coupled to two baths. Figure 2 compares the marginal position distribution derived theoretically versus numerically. Figure 3 shows the analytical marginal position distribution for varying bead masses.
paper_structure: The paper develops the dynamics using Langevin equations, analyzes the steady-state covariance matrix, derives key thermodynamic quantities like heat flux and entropy production, and culminates in establishing kinetic temperatures as the universal variables governing the system's thermodynamics.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework connecting energy, transport, and entropy via kinetic temperatures provides a powerful, generalizable tool for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in complex physical systems, relevant to open quantum systems modeling.
